title: I really want to watch Sergei Bondarchuk's adaptation of War & Peace. Should I read the novel first?

commenti.body: I'd say the only really challenging aspect of the novel is the philosophical treaty that bookends the novel. Besides that, it's a highly enjoyable book that is hilariously satirical, enthralling in its depiction of the Napoleonic Wars, and offers some truly profound character arcs. Basically, this is a long-winded way of saying that you should read the book first.

Read the novel, don't get intimidated by the number of pages. Reading War and Peace is one of the most satisfying and unforgettable experiences I ever had with a piece of art.

The film is great too, but the level of intimacy you get with the characters from reading the novel gets a bit lost. Still a great film, just a different experience.

Tolstoi must be experienced in literary form, both War and Peace and Anna Karenina are masterpieces.

The only challenging aspect from the novel are the philosophic passages, but you understand also Tolstoi's  views about life and human behavior.

Can you recommend me a translation? I wanted to start reading it two weeks ago but half the paragraphs were in French (because that's what the characters are speaking) with the English translation at the bottom of the page.

I don't need a dumned down version I just need one that I can clearly follow the narrative. I also tried the BBC audioplay but it assumes you've read the novel and doesn't explain everything well. I wanted to read the book before watching the film as well, I just need a good translation.

The movies actually prompted me to read the novel.  I found it interesting that way as it gave some more background to events and storylines.  However you decide to do it, both are definitely worth the time you will need to invest in it.  I did not find it a very hard novel to read.
The paragraphs and pages in French are a feature of the Russian original though, reading extended parts of it through translated footnotes is true to the original experience if you don't know French
That's not what I'm looking for. I saw translations out there that just translate the French into English. I just don't know if they are any good or not.
Anthony Briggs' translation does a great job making the text understandable for a modern audience and if I remember correctly has minimal french .
Just ordered it on Amazon. Thanks!

I'd read the novel first for sure. I personally also think you judge the performance of the director when judging a piece of movie, which wouldn't be possible unless you know what the director wanted to do, did, and didn't do compared to the work he based his film off.

[Have you tried the penguin edition?](https://www.amazon.co.uk/War-Peace-Penguin-Popular-Classics-ebook/dp/B0033805UG/ref=sr_1_4?crid=DCQO6U6X045F&dib=eyJ2IjoiMSJ9.Fz5K_WaZDg0KO4inNkTRSaoeUNOa5e19Rq4DfzSv8r1_WioqohujPV5aBbbupc1rwupQgnFB9g85BFerqzATGWPMEkKkPx_QTK76QGhJmsPGsdqcXGgCKVFx-X8_Z2K8FaerlhuxbvaVVLCgS5_OP4r2HdxUee3DHGEVBAaTDC1EDWiN5G6s5blz6dPn2LyDbQu9nbR9E6V0OwzeApUutsWRhUQfPaLTl3Lmoqljj0M.YZYoZA5SwLeTac36c6kHYFvMMsDw4lUw9AW8gZo09uI&dib_tag=se&keywords=war+and+peace&qid=1728378956&sprefix=war+and+pe%2Caps%2C132&sr=8-4)

I read the 2007 English translation and found it a very accessible book.  Long to be sure, but very engaging. 

I have never seen that film.  I did see the  miniseries in English with  Paul Dano and it had been awhile since I read the book and it seemed to hit  the major story incidents pretty well.

>The only challenging aspect from the novel are the philosophic passages

This wasn't my experience at all. For me, by far the most challenging aspect was keeping track of [all the characters](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_War_and_Peace_characters). I had to abandon it about 200 pages in, because by that point I had no idea who I was reading about. This meant that I never really got to the philosophical passages, but from skimming them briefly they seemed much more straightforward than the narrative.

(But then again, I was trying to read it on a Kindle beside my daughter while she was in the neonatal care unit, which in retrospect was perhaps a bit ambitious...)

You do not have to read the novel first but I would reccomend giving it a shot, outside of its length it is actually a relatively easy read for about the first 2/3rd to 3/4s then get a little more difficult. Several versions will also have footnotes to help you out with some of the context.

However, it really is not a huge a deal, you will still enjoy the film and still get most of the story but will be missing some subtext and character relationships

Simply put, they’re no good. Good translators will attempt to preserve the structure and feel of the original. That includes translating the native language while keeping passages in French that were originally in French. Maintaining that language shift actually informs your experience and interpretation of the work. Russia is fighting a war against France, and all these Russian nobles are speaking with each other in French, not Russian. It’s an interesting social commentary.
Pevear and Volkonsky is the one I’d go with. I’ve read it twice in different translations, and the P&V translation flowed much better and included very insightful explanatory footnotes.
I also recommend the Pevear and Volkonsky.

Alright so I think this depends on what you’re looking for; Tolstoy approved of the Maude translation but they don’t translate the French in some versions. The Oxford world classics is the one to get if you want them.


The Briggs translation is also very neat and good although not as good imo. However it is easier to read and French in translated to English. I don’t like it as much as it’s too westernized such as the soldiers calling each other mates lol. Either way these two are usually the more well received ones especially over P&V and Garnett’s translation.

I haven't read the book but the movie is one of the best I've ever seen - stupendous in its scale but more importantly brilliant in its direction. You don't have to read the novel first, but I suspect it will help a lot to enjoy the film. I suspect watching the film will also help you enjoy the book and give you an anchor to follow all the characters. It's not the kind of story that would be spoiled by knowing the plot. It's really just about characters living through a war torn period. So book or film first doesn't really matter.  Maybe watch the film, read the book, and watch the film again. It's sprawling and dense and worth a second watch.

I would strongly recommend reading War and Peace first. It is not overrated or anything of the sort - it stands as a key achievement in human creativity.

The film adaptation is brilliant as well.

It's a 1000 page book. That's already asking a lot. Then to expect me to read footnotes to understand what they're even saying is another accessibility layer. 

If I enjoy the book I'll read a more accurate translation next time because I already have a basic idea of how the story goes. I just want to absorb the events.
When it’s a language you don’t understand, you just read the footnotes, not the French. It’s not a huge energy barrier. The point is knowing what’s in French and what isn’t…
That's the one I ordered last night. Thanks!

Although it's not necessary by any means—Bondarchuk's film is a work of genius on its own—you should read it first. There's a reason it's so universally lauded; it's not really a challenging work, just lengthy, though it never feels like it's overstaying its welcome. Plus, having come from such a great work of literarure, it makes Bondarchuk's adaptation that much more impressive.

> Reading War & Peace isn't exactly considered a walk in park given its length and philosophical context of 19th century Russia apparently make it a challenging read. 

It's a surprisingly easy read.  The language isn't difficult at all.  The story, characters, and psychological insights will keep you turning the pages.

I suggest watching one minute, and then reading one page, and just keep alternating until you’ve completed both masterpieces. If anyone else has enjoyed them this way, please speak up!

Tolstoy's intended audience was the Russian intelligentsia in the 19th century, many of whom spoke French. You can only get the "original experience" if you speak both Russian and French. Translating the Russian is already departing from the "original experience." It seems absolutely ridiculous to leave the French untranslated. All that needs to be done to mark off the French parts is put them in italics.

War and Peace was basically required reading for all Russians at the time so the film assumes a basic understanding of the books contents. That’s not to say you won’t understand the film without it (ie. Aleksei German’s Hard to Be a God adaptation) but you might get a little lost because although the film is a fairly literal adaptation, the narrative is a bit too bulky to adapt neatly and some stuff falls through the cracks.
